content: In the 2018 guidelines, the effectiveness of pangenotypic direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for treating hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection was evaluated. Below are the findings and recommendations based on the data: Pangenotypic DAAs in HCV-Infected Adults Without Cirrhosis 1. Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir: Among treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced individuals, the pooled sustained virologic response (SVR) rates exceeded 96% for all six major HCV genotypes, except for genotype 3, which had an SVR rate of 89%. 2. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir: Pooled SVR rates exceeded 94% for all six major genotypes. For the rare genotype 5, two individuals treated achieved SVR. 3. Sofosbuvir/Daclatasvir: Pooled SVR rates exceeded 92% for genotypes 1, 2, 3, and 4. Observational data showed SVR rates of 88% for genotype 5 and 94% for genotype 6 after 12 weeks of treatment. Pangenotypic DAAs in HCV-Infected Adults With Compensated Cirrhosis 1. Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir: For individuals with cirrhosis, pooled SVR rates were 90% for genotype 1, 86% for genotype 2, and 88% for genotype 4. For genotype 3, SVR rates were 97% in treatment-naïve individuals and 90% in treatment-experienced individuals. Additional studies reported 100% SVR rates for genotypes 5 and 6 after 12 weeks of treatment. 2. Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir: SVR rates exceeded 94% for genotypes 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6. Two individuals with genotype 5 achieved SVR. 3. Sofosbuvir/Daclatasvir: Pooled SVR rates exceeded 93% for genotypes 1 and 2. For genotype 3, SVR rates ranged from 79% to 82% after 12 weeks but increased to 90% with 24 weeks of treatment. Observational data showed SVR rates of 92% for genotype 6 and over 98% for genotype 4. Safety of Pangenotypic DAAs Treatment discontinuation due to adverse events was very low (<1%) in both cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic individuals. Similar safety profiles were observed in treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced individuals. Rationale for Recommendations The Guidelines Development Group recommended pangenotypic DAAs for HCV treatment due to their clinical benefits and the potential to simplify care pathways. These regimens eliminate the need for expensive genotyping, streamline procurement and supply chains, and facilitate global treatment expansion. However, the group acknowledged that in some countries, non-pangenotypic regimens may still play a role, especially where HCV is predominantly caused by a single genotype or where pangenotypic formulations are not yet approved or available. Simplified Service Delivery for HCV Testing and Treatment 1. Decentralization: HCV testing and treatment should be delivered at peripheral health or community-based facilities, ideally at the same site, to increase access to care. This includes primary care, harm reduction sites, prisons, and HIV/ART clinics. 2. Integration: 3. Task Sharing: Training and mentoring of non-specialist healthcare workers and peer workers are recommended to expand service delivery. 4. Differentiated Care: A strategy to assess and address patient needs at different levels of care, with specialist referral for complex cases, is advised. 5. Community Engagement: Peer support and community involvement are essential to promote access to services and address stigma and discrimination. Feasibility and Equity Decentralized and integrated care models have been shown to improve access to HCV testing and treatment, particularly for marginalized populations such as people who inject drugs and prisoners. These models reduce transportation costs, waiting times, and stigma, while improving linkage to care and retention in treatment. Cost and Cost-Effectiveness Simplified decentralized care models are cost-effective compared to traditional specialist-led care. Studies have demonstrated reduced costs per patient and improved health outcomes with decentralized and integrated care delivery. Conclusion The adoption of pangenotypic DAAs and simplified service delivery models offers significant opportunities to expand HCV treatment access globally. These approaches are particularly beneficial for marginalized populations and can accelerate progress toward the elimination of HCV as a public health threat by 2030.
